Chapter 7: The Seduction of Stories—How Narratives Shape Belief.
People have always been natural storytellers. We take the messiness of life and spin it into tales, finding meaning where there might not be any at all. Why do we do this? Well, stories help us make sense of the world. They connect us with each other, and they give purpose to the everyday. But here's the thing—not all stories are innocent. Sometimes, the way we shape our narratives can lead us astray, especially when we're dealing with pure chance.
Picture a group of friends gathered around a table, swapping stories about how they met their partners or landed their dream jobs. Every story is sprinkled with twists of fate—tiny moments that, looking back, feel almost magical. It’s comforting, right? The idea that everything happens for a reason. But if you dig a little deeper, you'll see that luck played a much bigger role than anyone wants to admit.
Now, let’s step into the financial world for a moment. Here, stories are everywhere. A company’s success gets pinned on a visionary leader or a brilliant strategy. And when things fall apart? Suddenly, there’s a new story—full of blame, finger-pointing, and lessons learned. But so many of these stories are written after the fact, shaped to fit what happened. The truth? It’s usually a whole lot messier, tangled up with luck and randomness that rarely get mentioned.
Think about a young entrepreneur, inspired by all those legendary success stories. She dives headfirst into her new venture, convinced that if she just works hard enough and follows the right advice, she’ll make it big. But when things don’t go as planned, she’s left wondering what went wrong. The stories she believed never warned her about the wild card of chance.
Don’t get me wrong—stories have their place. They help us remember, they help us connect, and they make learning a whole lot easier. But it’s worth remembering that most stories are simplified. They’re edited, shaped by hindsight, and focused on the winners. The losers? They’re often left out, creating a distorted picture of how things really work.
Now, imagine a seasoned investor. He’s heard every narrative under the sun, and he’s learned to listen with a critical ear. Instead of just accepting the story, he asks, “What’s missing here? Who isn’t being talked about? And just how much did luck shape this outcome?” He isn’t looking for tidy explanations—he wants the bigger picture.
The truth is, the pull of a good story is hard to resist. But if you stay curious and just a little bit skeptical, you can start to see what’s hiding beneath the surface. That’s where you’ll find the real story—one that’s a little messier, but a whole lot closer to the truth.
